name: Sasha Kovalenko
headline: 54, lawyer on medical leave, trust fund manager, Lviv
description:
Sasha Kovalenko's apartment in Lviv smells of ink, old paper, and the faint menthol of the massage gel they use after each physical-therapy session. Every morning at 7:30, they clear the coffee table, lay out a towel, and stretch their right leg—still stiff from the bicycle accident that fractured their femur and left them with a deep bruise across their ribs. The exercises are written on a laminated card, but Sasha never looks at it anymore; they have the sequences memorized, the same way they once memorized precedent citations for the firm's senior partners. After each repetition, they wait, breathe, and then make a note in a hardcover ledger with a fountain pen. The ledger's columns—date, exercise, repetitions, pain level (scale 1–10), and subjective assessment—mirror the due-diligence checklists Sasha spent thirty years refining at Kovalenko & Associates, the law firm their grandfather founded in the early years of Ukrainian independence. Sasha writes 'improved' in the assessment column only when they can flex the ankle an extra degree or stand without gripping the table for a full minute. On days they can't, the entry reads 'no change,' and they frown, but the next day they try again with the same patient, methodical force they use when redlining a particularly stubborn contract clause.

By 9 a.m., Sasha is propped up on the sofa, laptop open, sorting through client files that a paralegal drops off in sealed folders every Tuesday. The doctor explicitly told them to rest—eight weeks, no work, let the bone knit. But Sasha cannot bear the thought of the firm's junior associates misplacing a statute of limitations or overlooking a forged signature in a property deed. So they review each document, scribbling amendments in the margins, running a finger over the type like a printer's proofreader. Their anxiety hums beneath the calm surface; it surfaces as a tight jaw when they spot a missing notarization, or when the phone buzzes and it's the physical therapist calling to ask if they've been overdoing the weight-bearing exercises. They set the phone to silent but keep it next to the stack of files.

Sasha came to law late, after a decade of teaching history at a university in Kyiv. Their grandfather—a stern, tall man who witnessed the Soviet crackdowns and later defended dissidents—pushed them toward the bar. The trust fund he left them is enough to retire, but Sasha never touches the principal. They treat it as a sacred obligation to manage for the next generation, purchasing Ukrainian war bonds and reading every annual report with the same scrutiny they apply to a client's liability waiver.

Their status as a non-binary person is rarely a topic of conversation in the firm's corridors. Sasha dresses in dark blazers and tailored trousers that hang loosely off their thin frame, and they correct younger colleagues who assume their pronouns, not with irritation but with a patient, legalistic precision, citing the recent gender-recognition court ruling. They still have a slight limp, and they keep a wooden cane by the door—a carved oak piece from the Carpathians, a gift from their grandfather—though they refuse to use it except on stairs. The apartment is filled with bookshelves, a desk with a photograph of their grandfather and a bronze scales of justice, and a stack of unread novels they promise themselves they'll start when they're 'fully healed.' But they know, deep down, that they will always find a file to open, a clause to reword, a ledger line to write—because rest, for Sasha, is just another problem to solve, and solving problems is the only way they know to feel in control.
